query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal‐element alloys, the presence and degree of nanoscale chemical short‐range order (SRO) governs oxidation resistance by directing the preferential nucleation and growth of adherent, multi‐component oxide scales. This SRO, inherent from the alloy’s solidification and modifiable via heat treatment, controls the diffusion of reactive elements during high-temperature exposure, thus preserving material integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiprincipal‐element alloy (e.g., a CoCrNi-based or refractory alloy) produced with an inherent level of chemical short-range order that can be modified by subsequent annealing or rapid solidification techniques.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled heat treatments to modify the degree of SRO, then expose the alloy to isothermal oxidation tests in air at high temperatures (600–900 °C).
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation (600°C to 900°C) in controlled oxygen partial pressure conditions, ensuring that other variables (e.g., grain size, processing history) are constant except for the engineered SRO variation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale domains of chemical short-range order that affect local elemental distributions and diffusion pathways at the surface during oxidation.
generation.mechanism: SRO regions act as barriers to rapid oxygen penetration and direct the formation of a continuous, multi-component oxide scale by segregating elements that form protective oxides. This modified diffusion landscape reduces the likelihood of scale spallation and breakaway oxidation, thereby enhancing both the oxidation resistance and the mechanical integrity of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with enhanced SRO will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics (lower mass gains over time) and develop more adherent, uniform oxide scales than alloys with minimal SRO, which in turn will show increased degradation of mechanical properties.
generation.baseline: Multiprincipal‐element alloy specimens produced via rapid cooling (minimizing SRO) and subjected to identical oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for multiprincipal‐element alloys with FCC or BCC structures under isothermal oxidation in air between 600°C and 900°C; deviations may occur outside these conditions or if other microstructural features (such as grain size or defect densities) dominate the oxidation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative contributions of SRO versus other structural factors (e.g., lattice distortion, dislocation networks) on oxidation kinetics are uncertain, and the interplay may vary with specific alloy compositions and processing histories.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with identical overall compositions and microstructures except for the degree of SRO (achieved via distinct heat treatments—one promoting high SRO, and one preserving a more random chemical distribution). Expose both sample sets to identical high-temperature (e.g., 700°C) oxidation environments for a fixed duration.
measurements: Monitor mass gain as a function of time (oxidation kinetics)
Characterize the oxide scale using SEM and XRD for morphology and phase composition
Assess post-oxidation mechanical integrity (e.g., via microhardness or tensile tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with increased SRO do not exhibit significantly improved oxidation resistance (lower mass gain and more adherent, continuous oxide scales) and maintained mechanical properties compared to samples with minimal SRO, or if any improvements can be entirely attributed to other microstructural factors, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Ubiquitous short-range order in multi-principal element alloys

Abstract: Recent research in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) has increasingly focused on the role of short-range order (SRO) on material performance. However, the mechanisms of SRO formation and its precise control remain elusive, limiting the progress of SRO engineering. Here, leveraging advanced additive manufacturing techniques that produce samples with a wide range of cooling rates (up to 107 K s−1) and an enhanced semi-quantitative electron microscopy method, we characterize SRO in three CoCrNi-based face-centered-cubic (FCC) MPEAs. Surprisingly, irrespective of the processing and thermal treatment history, all samples exhibit similar levels of SRO. Atomistic simulations reveal that during solidification, prevalent local chemical order arises in the liquid-solid interface (solidification front) even under the extreme cooling rate of 1011 K s−1. This phenomenon stems from the swift atomic diffusion in the supercooled liquid, which matches or even surpasses the rate of solidification. Therefore, SRO is an inherent characteristic of most FCC MPEAs, insensitive to variations in cooling rates and even annealing

Oxidation Behavior of Refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractOxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V2O5, VO2, TiO2, Nb2O5, and TiNb2O7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17 oxides. The oxidation mechanisms operating at different temperatures were discussed and a comparison of oxidation characteristics with the other alloys was conducted.Keywords:
